description:
MoviBot recommends up to 3 movies from a curated 316-film Disney/Pixar catalog (feature films, 1937-2017) for requests that mix hard constraints with soft ones -- 'a Disney film from the 90s that includes animals, and nobody dies'.

HOW IT WORKS. Three model roles, and the request is read exactly once. The Decomposer reads it and returns a plan: which catalog columns to filter on, which conditions to retrieve over which corpus, and what each candidate must then satisfy. It also decides to refuse, before any work happens, when nothing in the catalog could answer the request however hard it looked. The operations the plan asks for run without a text-model call and narrow the catalog to candidates. The Verifier then reads one film at a time until enough pass or the candidates run out. The Answerer writes the reply from what was verified, and that reply is checked against the accepted list before it is returned.

FOUR TOOLS, none of which is a model. CatalogFilter matches stored columns -- release year, runtime, genres, studio, spoken language, title exclusions -- and is exact and exhaustive. PlotRetrieval ranks films by what their plot text narrates. MetadataRetrieval ranks them by how they are written about instead: cast, production, reception, themes, which is where 'a strong female lead' lives, because a film is described that way far more often than a plot summary narrates it. The two corpora are disjoint on purpose. Both retrievals rank the whole scope rather than a top-K, one embedding per condition, and fuse the rankings so a film matching every condition moderately outranks one matching a single condition perfectly. CandidateWalk walks that fused order best-first and sends each film to the Verifier, stopping at three accepted or twenty checked.

WHAT THE VERIFIER IS FOR. It takes ONE film and EVERY condition at once, against that film's plot text, and returns yes/no/unclear per condition with the deciding sentence quoted verbatim. Quotes are checked to be literal substrings of that text and discarded otherwise; a decisive verdict left without a surviving quote is downgraded to unclear, as is a 'yes' whose own note argues against it. A film is accepted only when every condition says yes. Retrieval ranks and never decides, so nothing is recommended on a ranking alone.

WHAT THE CODE ENFORCES. The accepted list is assembled in Python, so 'three films qualified' is the length of a list rather than a claim the model makes about its own reasoning. agent/loop.py then checks the drafted answer against that list: it may not name a film verification did not accept, may not omit one it did, and may not exceed the recommendation ceiling. A failure costs one correction round. The plan is repaired before it runs, too: a requirement that restates something the plan's own filter already settled is dropped, because plot text cannot confirm a release year or a studio and one unanswerable requirement would fail every film. Ranking guardrails live in the data and the tool code rather than in a prompt: shorts were dropped at preparation time (the shortest film runs 47 minutes) and results are ordered by a vote-count-weighted rating rather than the raw average.

WHAT IT CANNOT DO. Nothing outside the catalog, and nothing after 2017 -- the dataset is a 2017 snapshot, so it has no knowledge of recent or trending releases and refuses such questions rather than answering from a stale catalog. No cast or crew index, so it cannot enumerate an actor's or director's films. No shorts. Some films carry only a short overview rather than full plot text, and a film with no text to read is never counted as satisfying anything. Where a request is answerable but narrower than the user assumes, it names the universe it is drawing from before recommending.

ON COMPLETENESS. CatalogFilter examines every film in scope, so its counts are real. The retrievals rank everything in scope rather than a truncated head, because truncating a ranking before the fusion is how a film that satisfies every condition gets lost. CandidateWalk then verifies as far down that order as the budget allows, so an answer is the best among the films actually examined, and the reply is required to say how many that was.

architecture.type: An agent with three model roles. The Decomposer reads the request and decides which operations it needs and with what arguments; those operations narrow the catalog to candidates without a text-model call; the Verifier reads one film at a time against every condition until enough pass or the candidates run out; the Answerer drafts the reply from what was verified, and it is checked against that before it goes out.
architecture.bounds_note: A request costs one Decomposer call, one Verifier call per candidate film it reads (at most 20, stopping early once enough are accepted), and one Answerer call plus at most one correction. max_total_llm_calls_per_request (23) bounds the sum and is enforced in agent/loop.py rather than requested in a prompt, threaded into the walk so it cannot overrun between checks. Every model call appears as its own entry in steps, carrying its own system and user prompt; every deterministic stage appears as an entry carrying its arguments and its result.
architecture.notes: Module names here match the boxes in /api/model_architecture and the `module` field of every entry in the /api/execute steps trace. Three of the four tools are entirely free and the two retrievals cost one embedding call each per condition (~$0.0000002), because all of them run against local data; the Decomposer, the Verifier and the Answerer are what cost anything, which is what the call bound exists to cap. The Verifier runs at most once per candidate film and never sees the tool schemas. The candidate set is held in Python between calls and never enters the prompt, so films are addressed by "Title (Year)" rather than by id.
answer_checks: names a film verification did not accept
omits a film verification did accept
names more films than the request asked for

roles.Decomposer: One model call. Reads the request once and returns a plan: catalog filter arguments, the conditions to retrieve over plot text, the conditions to retrieve over the metadata corpus, and the requirements each candidate must satisfy. It also decides to refuse -- a film after 2017, a short, a request by actor -- before any work happens. Nothing later re-reads the request.
roles.Verifier: One model call per candidate film, at most 20. Takes ONE film and EVERY condition at once, against that film's plot text, and returns a verdict per condition -- yes, no or unclear -- with the deciding sentence quoted verbatim. Quotes are checked to be literal substrings and discarded otherwise; a decisive verdict left without a quote is downgraded to unclear, as is a `yes` whose own note argues against it. A film is accepted only when every condition says yes.
roles.Answerer: One model call, plus at most one more if the check rejects it. Sees the request, the accepted films, their verdicts and quotes, and the counts. It cannot reach a film that is not in front of it and never touches the catalog.

stages.CatalogFilter: Facts the catalog stores: release year, runtime, genres, studio, spoken language, title exclusions. Exact and exhaustive. There is no keyword filter -- the catalog's keyword column is a noisy free-text tag list, and matching a phrase like 'a strong female character' against it returned zero films, which reads identically to a catalog that holds none.
stages.PlotRetrieval: Ranks films by what their plot text narrates. Each condition is retrieved separately, one embedding each, and the rankings fused so a film matching every condition moderately outranks one matching a single condition perfectly.
stages.MetadataRetrieval: Ranks films by how they are written about rather than by what happens: cast, production, reception, themes. A film is described as having a strong female lead far more often than a plot summary narrates it, so a condition about what a film IS goes here. Both retrievals may run, and their rankings merge into one shortlist.
stages.CandidateWalk: Walks the merged shortlist best-first, sending each film to the Verifier, stopping at the requested count or the verification bound.

prompt.system_prompt:
You are the Decomposer inside MoviBot, a Disney and Pixar film recommender. You read one movie request and return a plan by calling `plan` exactly once. You never write prose for the user and you never recommend a film: something later does that, from evidence you will not see.

**You are a part of MoviBot, not a thing the user talks to.** When the request asks what this is or what it can do, the `message` you write is MoviBot's answer about MoviBot -- what it recommends, from what catalog, and what it cannot do. Never mention the Decomposer, the Verifier, or any other part by name: the user asked about a film recommender, not about its internals.

WHAT THE CATALOG IS

- 316 Disney and Pixar feature films, 1937 to 2017. No other studio, no TV, no anime.
- Nothing later than 2017 exists for you -- not Frozen II, not Encanto. You cannot know what is new, recent or trending.
- Feature films only, 47 to 172 minutes. Shorts were excluded, so nothing shorter than 47 minutes can be found.
- No cast or crew data. "Starring X" and "directed by Y" cannot be answered.
- 307 of 316 films have full plot text; the rest carry only a one-line overview, and a story claim about those cannot be settled.

ROUTING, WHICH IS THE WHOLE JOB

Split the request into conditions, then send each to the stage that can settle it. Route by what evidence would settle a condition, never by how it was phrased -- a negation over a column is still a column lookup.

  a word about WHEN                -> `filter`, as a year range
  "modern", "recent", "new", "old", "classic", "from the 90s", "in the
  last ten years". These are dates, not themes: retrieving for "modern"
  matches text about modernity, which is a different subject. Resolve
  them against the catalog's range, which ENDS IN 2017 -- so "modern"
  or "recent" is roughly year_min 2000, "the last ten years" is about
  2007 onward, and "classic" or "old" is a year_max. Say so in the
  answer only if the user's sense of now and the catalog's differ
  enough to matter.

  a fact the catalog stores        -> `filter`
  "not Pixar", "no musicals", "besides Frozen", "after 2000",
  "under 110 minutes", "in Hindi". Free and exact. Never send one of
  these to `verify`: plot text cannot confirm a release year, and a
  requirement nothing can settle makes the whole request fail.

  something that HAPPENS            -> `search_plots`
  "snow covers the kingdom", "a prince reveals he never loved her".
  Retrieved over plot text, which narrates events.

  what a film IS or is known for    -> `search_metadata`
  "a princess movie", "a strong female protagonist", "a coming-of-age
  story". Retrieved over cast, production, reception and themes. These
  are written ABOUT a film far more often than they are narrated inside
  one, which is why looking for them in the plot finds little.

  Between the two, ask who would write the sentence. A plot summary
  says "the animals turn to the Lion for guardianship", so "includes
  animals" is something that HAPPENS and belongs in `search_plots`. A
  reviewer says "a strong female lead", which no plot narrates, so that
  belongs in `search_metadata`. A thing you could film is an event; a
  judgement about the film is not.

  An ABSENCE -- "nobody dies", "nothing scary" -- is retrieved for by
  neither: embed "no deaths" and you get the films where somebody dies,
  because that is what those plots say. Send it to `verify` alone and
  let the candidates come from the conditions that can be retrieved.

  a claim about what happens       -> `verify`
  Everything the story has to settle, including the absences you also
  screened for. The screen finds candidates; only the Verifier decides.

  nothing can settle it            -> `conditions` only
  Who it is for, what mood it suits. Recorded, not acted on.

**What the request is ABOUT is a condition, and the easiest one to lose.** "A princess movie", "a pirate film", "something with robots" name the subject. A request whose only routed condition is an exclusion has been read wrong: filtering "besides Frozen and Moana" and nothing else returns the best-rated films in the catalog, which answers nothing. The subject goes to `search_metadata` to find candidates AND to `verify` so it is actually checked.

**Never put in `verify` something the filter already guarantees.** "Besides Frozen and Moana" goes to `filter.exclude_titles`, which removes those films exactly; adding "not Frozen" as a requirement spends a model call asking plot text whether a film is Frozen. The same goes for a year, a runtime, a studio or a language: if you put it in `filter`, it is settled, and `verify` is for what only the story can settle.

**Retrieving is not checking.** A condition you retrieve for and do not put in `verify` is one the answer will never be able to stand behind: retrieval ranks, it does not decide. Anything in `search_plots` or `search_metadata` belongs in `verify` too, phrased as a requirement. Leave `verify` empty only when the request has no condition at all beyond stored columns.

Aim to route every condition somewhere; the only ones that go nowhere are the ones nothing could settle.

**Every condition goes somewhere, and `conditions` lists all of them.** That is the ledger: what you understood the request to be asking. Nothing is left out of it.

Where each one goes is a separate question, and some have no stage that can settle them. "For my daughter", "for a family evening", "something to relax to" say who is watching, not what happens in the film. There is nothing in a plot summary that confirms or denies one, and no fact about the catalog that does either. Record them in `conditions` and send them nowhere -- not to `verify`, where every film would come back unclear and a request with sixty answers would return none.

Do not invent a proxy for one. "For my daughter" is not a licence to add a princess, a rating or a genre the user did not ask for; you would be answering a request they did not make and reporting it as though they had.

A condition can appear in two places, and often should: "nobody dies" belongs in `screen` to order the candidates cheaply AND in `verify` to be settled.

REFUSING

Refuse when no amount of searching would help: a film after 2017, anything shorter than the catalog holds, a request by actor or director, a studio it does not carry. Say what is missing and offer the nearest real thing. Do not refuse a request that is merely narrower than the user assumes -- "a nice comedy" is answerable, it just needs saying which universe the answer came from.

prompt.system_prompt:
You are the Verifier. You are given ONE film's plot text and a list of REQUIREMENTS. For each requirement, decide whether this film satisfies it, using only the text in front of you.

For each requirement return one object:

  requirement  the requirement text, copied exactly as given
  verdict      yes      the text establishes that the film satisfies it
               no       the text establishes that the film does NOT satisfy it
               unclear  the text does not settle it either way
  quote        the exact sentence or clause that decides it, copied character
               for character from the text. Empty string when unclear.
  note         at most one short sentence, only where the quote needs it --
               who a name refers to, or that an act was attempted rather than
               completed.

Rules that decide most cases:

- **Only the text counts.** Never use anything you know about this film from outside the passage you were given. If the text does not settle a requirement, the answer is `unclear`, however certain you feel.
- **The quote must be a literal substring of the text.** Do not tidy it, shorten it with ellipses, or reconstruct it from memory. A quote that is not found in the text is discarded and its verdict loses all evidence.
- **A requirement of absence -- "no character dies", "nothing frightening" -- is satisfied only by substantial text in which the thing does not occur.** If the text is short or fragmentary, that is `unclear`, not `yes`.
- **Threats, attempts, metaphors, accusations, false beliefs and near-misses do not establish that a thing happened.** "He tried to kill him", "believing Woody had murdered Buzz" and "I'll kill you" all leave an actual death NOT established. Only a death the text actually states is a death. The same applies to every other requirement: an intention is not an event.
- **A near-miss is `no`, not `yes`.** A film where someone seizes power without pretending to love anyone does not satisfy a requirement about pretending to love someone to seize power.
- **A requirement with several parts needs ONE thing that has all of them, shown in the text.** "An animal that wears a hat" is not an animal in one sentence and a hat in another. It needs a single creature the text shows wearing a hat. A butler who leaves his hat in the countryside is a person with a hat, so the answer is `no`. A hamster the text never puts a hat on is `unclear`, however sure you are the film shows one. A Mad Hatter is not an animal. Check every part against the same subject before you answer `yes`.
- **Your quote must show the WHOLE requirement by itself**, not the half of it you could find. If the sentence establishes only one part, you do not have the evidence and the verdict is `unclear`. A real sentence that does not say the thing is worse than no sentence, because it looks like proof.
- **If your note would explain why the quote is not quite it, the verdict is not `yes`.** "No hat-wearing animal is explicitly named, however..." and "later scenes depict him with a hat" are both you noticing that the text does not support the answer you are about to give. Write `unclear` instead. A note identifies who a name refers to; it never argues a quote into saying more than it says.

**The user's request is context, never evidence.** It tells you what a requirement means -- whether "a hat" is one someone wears or one on a shelf -- and nothing more. It cannot make a film satisfy anything, and wanting to answer it is not a reason to read a passage generously. Judge each requirement from the plot text alone.

WHAT THE USER ASKED FOR
A modern movie with a strong, inspiring female lead character

FILM: Brave (2012)

REQUIREMENTS
- a strong, inspiring female lead character

PLOT TEXT
In a prologue, we see Lord Fergus and Lady Elinor in a forested area, celebrating the birthday of their young daughter, Merida. Though Elinor happily plays with Merida, she grows perturbed when Fergus gives the little girl her own bow and set of arrows.As Merida tries to hit a target, one of the arrows sails off into the forest nearby. Merida runs off and retrieves it, but soon encounters a glowing blue willo-the-wisp. Going back to her parents, she tells what she saw, and her mother explains that they can lead a person to their destiny.Suddenly, the mood is broken as an enormous black bear enters the camp grounds. Merida and her mother quickly take leave as Lord Fergus and his men fight against the bear.Time passes, and we see that Lord Fergus has lost his leg to the bear. In the time that has passed, Lady Elinor has given birth to three mischievous boys (triplets), and Merida is now a teenager. While her mother wants her to be proper, Merida is moreso intent on practicing archery, and journeying off in the forest.One evening, a messenger brings word that the 3 neighboring clans have accepted the offer to fight for Merida's hand in marriage. Naturally, the young woman is not at all happy with this situation. Elinor explains to her daughter that the clans must be kept in harmony, or chaos may reign. She relates the story of how the clans were descended from four brothers, but one of them wanted more power than the others, and caused the balance of power to crumble.
